blurb: Proposition 132 would make distributing, manufacturing, dispensing, or selling any amount of fentanyl a level 1 drug felony, with a required prison sentence of 8–32 years. Backed by [Advance Colorado](https://whoisadvancecolorado.org/), it responds to overdose deaths with longer sentences rather than proven prevention and treatment. Effective responses include low-barrier counseling and medication, long-term treatment, recovery housing, evidence-based drug education, naloxone, and drug-checking tools.

measure title: Proposition 133: Penalties for Human Trafficking of a Minor
blurb: Proposition 133 would increase the penalty for child sex trafficking from a class 2 to a class 1 felony and require life in prison without parole. Legislative Council Staff projects it would not produce additional convictions. But trafficking survivors coerced into recruiting or managing other victims could face that mandatory sentence, with no judicial discretion to consider their circumstances. A fiscal estimate puts annual prison costs at $180,000, rising to $540,000 by 2043; the estimate’s baseline year needs verification.

Proposition 134 would restrict transgender students’ participation in school sports, while Proposition 135 would prohibit certain surgeries for minors. Both measures are backed by Protect Kids Colorado, which also sponsored the two proposals targeting transgender youth. They use state policy to restrict young people’s participation in school and access to care. The Green New Deal is for *ALL* peoples, not most.

Proposition 136 would cap Colorado’s individual and corporate income tax rates at 4.4%, their current rate. If it and Amendment 87 both pass, the cap could put the graduated income tax in legal jeopardy. It could also shield corporations from future rate increases and limit revenue for education, transportation, health care, and other services during a budget shortfall. Colorado has the nation’s 39th most regressive tax system, with wealthier residents paying a smaller share of income in state and local taxes.

measure title: Proposition 137: Designate Sporting Goods Sales Tax Revenue for Conservation
blurb: Proposition 137 would exempt about $175 million in sporting-goods sales tax revenue from the TABOR cap and direct it to wilderness conservation, wildfire mitigation, watershed restoration, and outdoor recreation. When revenue exceeds the cap, these funds would not affect existing programs. When revenue is below the cap, however, the measure could reduce General Fund resources available for other programs by about $175 million. If Proposition NN also passes, the state may remain below the cap, making that tradeoff more likely.

measure title: Amendment 81: Law Enforcement Reporting Requirements to Federal Authorities
blurb: Amendment 81 would require state and local law enforcement to contact ICE within 72 hours if someone suspected of lacking legal status is charged with a violent crime or has a prior felony conviction. It would apply based on a charge, before conviction, and override current state limits on ICE involvement. People could be exposed to ICE if they cannot prove their status within 72 hours; judgments based on appearance or accent could also invite racial profiling.

Amendment 82 would establish a constitutional right for consumers to buy natural gas for home or business use and for utilities to sell it. Brought by [Advance Colorado](http://whoisadvancecolorado.org), the measure could make it easier for fossil-fuel companies to sue over clean-energy policies and public-health protections. Natural gas emits greenhouse gases, and enshrining its use could restrict state and local efforts to cut emissions, improve air quality, and transition to cleaner energy.

measure title: Amendment 83: Constitutional Right to Hunt and Fish
blurb: Amendment 83 would prioritize hunting and fishing over other approaches to wildlife management and limit Colorado Parks and Wildlife’s ability to respond to new science, protect habitat, and consider other species. Its undefined phrase “traditional methods” could allow baiting and steel-jawed leghold traps, practices Colorado voters have previously banned. With climate change making wildlife and habitat conditions less predictable, the state needs flexibility for science-based conservation.

Amendment 84 would require voters to sign their mail-ballot envelope and provide the last four digits of a Social Security number, Colorado driver’s license, or REAL ID. If the information is missing or does not match state records, voters would need to take additional steps within a limited time or their ballot would not count. A 2024 study of states with strict voter ID laws found nearly half of transgender people lacked ID matching their name or gender identity. The measure could also exclude an estimated 15–25% of older, Black, Latino, and lower-income voters who lack accepted ID.

Amendment 85 would require ballot questions to be written at an eighth-grade reading level and limit additional language required by state law. This could remove information explaining how tax changes affect different income groups and public budgets. For example, Proposition GG requires an income-tax measure to include a table showing effects by income level, while HB 21-1321 requires ballot language describing impacts on state and local budgets. Clear language should not come at the cost of that context.

Amendment 86 would add steps to redrawing congressional districts between censuses: proposals would go through Colorado’s independent redistricting commission and require approval by the state Supreme Court. Maps favoring one party are already prohibited, and Colorado already has an independent commission. The added requirements could make it harder for citizen-led efforts to respond to mid-decade redistricting, such as Texas’s 2025 effort ahead of the 2026 midterms.

Amendment 87 would establish six state income-tax brackets, raise taxes on higher-income households, and lower them for Coloradans earning under $1 million. All new revenue would go to health care, child care, and education, helping avoid cuts amid a projected state budget shortfall. The measure gives the legislature flexibility within those categories. Its specified revenue uses do not include climate programs.

measure title: Proposition NN: TABOR Revenue Cap Increase for K-12 Education
blurb: Proposition NN would raise the TABOR revenue cap by the $4.6 billion currently spent on K–12 education, allowing the state to keep revenue above the current cap and spend it on K–12 education and related programs such as child care and preschool. It would not raise taxes and would require annual public audits. The proposal estimates $520 million in additional education funding next year and cites an education shortfall of $3.5 billion, or about $4,000 per pupil.

measure title: Ballot Issue 7A: Colorado Connector Sales Tax
blurb: Ballot Issue 7A would impose a 0.333% sales tax in the Front Range Passenger Rail District to build and operate the Colorado Connector. Service is planned to start with three daily trains between Denver and Fort Collins in 2029, eventually expanding to 10 trains daily north and eight south to Pueblo. The measure also funds a local-return program for station-area improvements. Passenger rail offers a lower-carbon alternative to driving.

Denver Public Schools’ Issue 4A would raise $44 million annually through a mill levy override. Of that, $25.8 million would fund a $1,750 raise for every full-time DPS employee, plus incentives for educators in high-poverty schools and hard-to-fill roles such as bilingual teachers and school psychologists. Remaining funds would support student mental health, special education, and career and technical education. The proposal is estimated to cost about $72 a year in property taxes for a median-priced Denver home valued at roughly $625,000.

measure title: Denver Referred Measure 2H: Wage-Rights Enforcement in the Auditor’s Office
blurb: Since 1950, Denver’s Auditor’s Office has enforced wage laws. In the past five years, it has collected more than $9 million and helped vindicate the rights of over 15,000 workers through thousands of investigations. Measure 2H clarifies that the Auditor may continue enforcing wage laws, including minimum-wage, overtime, sick-leave, worker-classification, and anti-retaliation protections. It does not expand the office’s authority; it aligns the charter with existing law and practice.

measure title: Denver Referred Measure 2I: Budget and Appropriation Process
blurb: Measure 2I would let Denver prepare its budget every two years instead of annually, while City Council would still approve spending each year. The city could use a one-year budget during fiscal uncertainty. Proponents Councilmembers Shontel Lewis, Amander Sawyer, and Stacie Gilmore say the change would allow more time for planning and public comment and provide greater certainty for agencies and others relying on city funding. Denver’s 2025 budget crisis led to about 170 city employee layoffs and the cancellation of hundreds of open positions.

measure title: Denver Referred Measure 2J: Civil Service Commission and Department of Safety
blurb: Measure 2J would change Denver Charter rules for hiring, management, and discipline in the police and fire services. It would extend the public safety manager’s review period for discipline from 15 calendar days to 20 business days, lift caps on command staff, and remove the U.S.-citizenship requirement for Civil Service Commission members. It would move hiring rules into city ordinances, remove the vague “good moral character” qualification, use gender-neutral language, and eliminate a longevity-pay provision already covered by collective bargaining agreements.

measure title: Denver Referred Measure 2K: Xcel Franchise and Energy Partnership Agreements
blurb: Measure 2K would approve a 20-year franchise and companion Energy Partnership Agreement, giving Xcel the exclusive right to use Denver streets and rights-of-way to provide electric and natural-gas service. Amid rate hikes and unsatisfactory service, the city should seek a shorter term and stronger benefits for Denver residents while exploring public power.
